key_finding: deltaHED, a metric quantifying evolutionary divergence between germline and tumor-acquired HLA class I alleles, was associated with higher TMB and neoantigen load yet predicted worse PFS and OS under PD-1 blockade across three cancer types (RM/NPC, melanoma, ESCC). Mechanistic link to antigen-processing mutations is correlative
ESCC cohort received combination with chemotherapy, complicating interpretation
surprising_why: Contradicts the prevailing TMB/neoantigen-centric view: although high deltaHED tracked with higher TMB and neoantigen burden, it predicted worse rather than better PD-1 outcomes, suggesting HLA evolutionary divergence can mark immune escape rather than broad presentation capacity.

cSCC-specific — generalization untested

key_finding: Transient upregulation of PD-1 on clonally expanding human CD4+ and CD8+ T cells protects them from premature restimulation-induced cell death (RICD) by attenuating proximal TCR and CD28 signaling and modulating pro/anti-apoptotic protein expression. outcome: PD-1 signaling conferred apoptosis resistance to restimulated effector T cells, particularly PD-1^hi clonally expanding populations

No in vivo tumor or patient data
Mechanistic implications for PD-1 blockade-induced T cell loss are inferred

key_finding: WES of ccRCC from 35 anti-PD-1-treated patients identified LOF mutations in PBRM1 (PBAF SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling subunit) as enriched in clinical responders (P=0.012), validated in an independent cohort of 63 ccRCC patients (P=0.0071). intervention: nivolumab / anti-PD-1 (± anti-CTLA-4 in validation)
outcome: clinical benefit (response/PFS)
effect_size: PBRM1 LOF enriched in clinical benefit group in discovery (P=0.012, n=35) and validation (P=0.0071, n=63) cohorts

caveats: Small discovery cohort with modest p-values
ccRCC is TMB-low; signal may reflect unique renal biology
Direct causal experiments in syngeneic models limited
surprising_why: Subsequent larger analyses (Braun et al. 2020 Nat Med on CheckMate-009/010/025, IMmotion150/151) have failed to cleanly replicate PBRM1 as a predictor of ICI benefit in ccRCC — some cohorts show no association or opposite trends. A classic landmark-biomarker replicability failure.

human_study.effect_value: enriched among responders

key_finding: In vivo pooled CRISPR-Cas9 screen in B16 melanoma across 2,368 genes identified Ptpn2 loss in tumor cells as a sensitizer to anti-PD-1, acting by amplifying IFN-γ/JAK-STAT signaling to increase antigen presentation. intervention: CRISPR knockout of tumor-expressed genes (notably Ptpn2) + anti-PD-1/GVAX
outcome: Ptpn2-null tumors showed markedly enhanced rejection under checkpoint blockade; IFN-γ pathway KOs conferred resistance
effect_size: Ptpn2 sgRNAs strongly depleted from treated tumors (log2 FC ~-2 to -3); resistance hits (Jak1, Stat1, B2m, Tap1) strongly enriched

confidence.reasoning: Large unbiased in vivo screen with arrayed validation, orthogonal mechanistic follow-up, and concordance with prior human genetics. PTPN2 since validated clinically (ABBV-514-class inhibitors in trials).

caveats: Single tumor line (B16) with GVAX+anti-PD-1
Library covered only 2,368 genes, not genome-wide
Stromal/host modifiers not captured
surprising_why: PTPN2 had not previously been nominated as a tumor-intrinsic immune-evasion phosphatase; identifying a druggable negative regulator of IFN-γ signaling in tumor cells (rather than T cells) reframed PTPN2/PTP1B as oncology targets.

key_finding: Tumor-intrinsic WNT/β-catenin activation causes T-cell exclusion from the melanoma microenvironment and primary resistance to anti-PD-L1/anti-CTLA-4. In TCGA melanoma, β-catenin activation anti-correlated with a CD8 signature; in Braf/Pten/CAT-STA autochthonous mice, β-catenin-active tumors failed to recruit CD103+ Batf3+ DCs (via reduced CCL4), preventing T-cell priming.
intervention: Genetic β-catenin activation in autochthonous murine melanoma; anti-PD-L1 + anti-CTLA-4
outcome: β-catenin-active tumors non-T-cell-inflamed, lacked DC recruitment, refractory to dual checkpoint blockade
effect_size: ~48% of non-T-cell-inflamed human melanomas showed active β-catenin vs minimal activation in inflamed tumors; near-complete loss of intratumoral CD8 and ICI efficacy in β-catenin-active mice

confidence.reasoning: Coupled human genomic correlation (TCGA) with causal autochthonous mouse genetics and mechanistic dissection to CCL4/Batf3-DC recruitment. Extended to other tumor types; validated by multiple labs.

caveats: β-catenin activation is one of several drivers of the 'cold' phenotype — not necessary or sufficient across cohorts
Clinical translation of WNT inhibitors + ICI limited by toxicity
Autochthonous model uses single driver combination (BRAF/PTEN)
surprising_why: Reframed a classical developmental/oncogenic pathway as a direct cause of immune exclusion via impaired DC recruitment, at a time when resistance was largely framed around T-cell-intrinsic exhaustion. Subsequent clinical cohorts have found weaker and more context-dependent correlations between β-catenin activation and ICI non-response than the mouse model predicted.

key_finding: PTEN loss in melanoma activates PI3K-AKT, increases immunosuppressive cytokines (VEGF, CCL2), reduces autophagy-dependent T-cell killing, and decreases intratumoral T-cell infiltration. PTEN loss correlated with poorer TIL expansion and worse anti-PD-1 outcomes in a small cohort; a selective PI3Kβ inhibitor restored sensitivity in mice.
intervention: Genetic PTEN loss in melanoma models; PI3Kβ inhibitor (GSK2636771) + anti-PD-1 or anti-CTLA-4
outcome: PTEN-null tumors had reduced CD8 infiltration and impaired ICI response; PI3Kβ inhibition rescued efficacy in vivo

confidence.reasoning: Mechanism triangulated across human tumor samples, isogenic cell lines, and syngeneic mouse models with pharmacologic rescue. PTEN-loss–ICI resistance association replicated in melanoma and pan-cancer analyses.

caveats: Human cohort small and retrospective
Clinical PI3Kβ + ICI combinations have produced mixed early-phase results with toxicity limiting synergy
Effect of PTEN loss on ICI response is context-specific across histologies

human_study.effect_value: reduced intratumoral CD8, worse PFS

key_finding: WES/RNA-seq of pretreatment melanoma biopsies (n=38) under anti-PD-1 defined the IPRES (Innate anti-PD-1 Resistance) transcriptional signature — coordinated upregulation of EMT, cell adhesion, ECM remodeling, angiogenesis, and wound-healing genes — in innately resistant tumors. Higher TMB and BRCA2 mutations associated with response; MAPK-inhibitor programs overlapped with IPRES, suggesting non-genomic MAPKi cross-resistance.
intervention: Anti-PD-1 monotherapy (pembrolizumab/nivolumab) in metastatic melanoma
outcome: IPRES-high tumors enriched among non-responders; signature recurrent across independent cancer cohorts
effect_size: High TMB associated with improved OS (modest P-value); IPRES separated responders from non-responders in discovery cohort

caveats: Small discovery cohort; response definitions not harmonized across later validation
IPRES overlaps heavily with TGF-β/EMT/stromal signatures and may not add orthogonal info beyond CD8 or TGF-β signatures
BRCA2 association not consistently replicated
Bulk transcriptomics conflates tumor and stromal signals
surprising_why: IPRES catalyzed the EMT/wound-healing axis of ICI resistance concept, but subsequent validation has been mixed: as a predictive biomarker it has underperformed relative to CD8 TIL, PD-L1, TMB, and broader TGF-β/fibroblast signatures. A landmark hypothesis refined rather than confirmed.

key_finding: In KRAS-mutant lung adenocarcinoma, co-mutations in STK11/LKB1 define a 'KL' subgroup exhibiting primary resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade. KL tumors had markedly lower response and shorter PFS/OS despite comparable TMB, and were enriched for PD-L1-negative, non-T-cell-inflamed microenvironment; Stk11 loss in syngeneic Kras-mutant mouse LUAC was causally sufficient.
intervention: PD-1/PD-L1 blockade (nivo, pembro, atezo) in KRAS-mutant NSCLC stratified by STK11 and TP53; mouse Kras/Stk11 LOF
outcome: KL ORR 7.4% (SU2C) and 0% (CheckMate-057) vs 35.7%/57.1% for KP; STK11/LKB1 strongest negative correlate of PD-L1 positivity in TMB-intermediate/high LUAC
effect_size: ORR 7.4% KL vs 35.7% KP (P<0.001); PFS and OS significantly shorter in KL

confidence.reasoning: Multi-cohort retrospective analysis (>900 LUAC genomics; 174 ICI outcomes) plus CheckMate-057 validation and causal mouse genetics. KL resistance phenotype independently replicated in subsequent NSCLC ICI datasets.

caveats: Retrospective ICI cohorts with heterogeneous regimens
CheckMate-057 KL subgroup extremely small (n=6)
STK11 alterations co-occur with KEAP1; disentangling contributions required later work
surprising_why: Established that a tumor-suppressor comutation — not TMB or PD-L1 alone — can be the dominant determinant of primary ICI resistance within a TMB-high histology, decoupling TMB from ICI response and reshaping NSCLC biomarker thinking.

human_study.effect_value: KL 7.4% vs KP 35.7% (SU2C); 0% vs 57.1% (CheckMate-057)

key_finding: In KEYNOTE-024 (305 patients, advanced NSCLC, PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, EGFR/ALK-wildtype), first-line pembrolizumab monotherapy significantly improved PFS and OS versus platinum-doublet chemotherapy with fewer grade 3-5 AEs — establishing PD-L1 high expression as a predictive biomarker enabling single-agent ICI as 1L standard of care in NSCLC.
intervention: Pembrolizumab 200 mg Q3W vs investigator-choice platinum-doublet, 1L, PD-L1 TPS ≥50%
outcome: Superior PFS and OS with pembro; higher ORR, longer DoR, lower toxicity

confidence.reasoning: Randomized phase 3, positive primary/secondary endpoints, FDA/EMA approval basis. 5-year follow-up (Reck 2021) confirmed durable OS benefit despite crossover.

caveats: Restricted to PD-L1 TPS ≥50%, EGFR/ALK-wildtype — not generalizable to PD-L1-low or driver-mutant NSCLC
Crossover (~66%) diluted OS benefit
Chemo control was investigator's choice, not a single regimen

human_study.effect_value: mPFS 10.3 vs 6.0 mo; HR 0.50

key_finding: Phase 3 trial of 676 previously treated HLA-A*0201+ metastatic melanoma patients: ipilimumab (3 mg/kg) ± gp100 peptide vaccine significantly improved OS vs gp100 alone — the first therapy ever to demonstrate OS benefit in metastatic melanoma and the registrational study for the first approved immune checkpoint inhibitor.
intervention: Ipilimumab 3 mg/kg Q3W × 4 ± gp100 peptide vaccine vs gp100 alone
outcome: mOS ~10 mo in ipi arms vs 6.4 mo with gp100 alone; durable long-term survival plateau in ~20% of ipi-treated patients
effect_size: Ipi+gp100 vs gp100: mOS 10.0 vs 6.4 mo (HR 0.68, P<0.001); ipi alone vs gp100: 10.1 vs 6.4 mo (HR 0.66, P=0.003)

confidence.reasoning: Randomized phase 3 with OS primary endpoint, confirmed by Robert 2011 (ipi + dacarbazine). Long-term pooled analyses show durable 20-26% OS plateau extending to 10 years, definitively establishing checkpoint blockade.

caveats: Restricted to HLA-A*0201+ patients
Control arm (gp100) now considered inadequate
3 mg/kg dose later shown inferior to 10 mg/kg for OS
irAEs novel, sometimes severe; 2.1% treatment-related deaths
surprising_why: Prior to this trial, no therapy had ever prolonged OS in metastatic melanoma despite decades of chemotherapy, IL-2, and vaccines. The durable survival plateau — a subset of patients effectively cured by releasing an endogenous T-cell response — was transformative and inaugurated the modern era of cancer immunotherapy.

key_finding: First large phase 1 trial of anti-PD-1 (BMS-936558, later nivolumab) in 296 patients with advanced solid tumors: durable objective responses in melanoma (28%), NSCLC (18%), and RCC (27%) with manageable irAEs. Pretreatment tumor PD-L1 IHC correlated with response (9/25 PD-L1+ vs 0/17 PD-L1− patients), providing the first clinical evidence that PD-L1 could serve as a predictive biomarker.
intervention: Nivolumab 0.1-10 mg/kg Q2W, phase 1 dose-escalation/expansion
outcome: Durable objective responses (≥1 year in 20/31 evaluable responders); immune-related AEs including pneumonitis (3 fatal cases)
effect_size: ORR 28% melanoma (26/94), 18% NSCLC (14/76), 27% RCC (9/33); grade 3/4 drug-related AEs 14%; PD-L1+ vs PD-L1− ORR 36% vs 0% (P=0.006)

confidence.reasoning: Large phase 1 with central pathology; results rapidly confirmed by CheckMate-017/-057/-066/-025 → broad regulatory approvals.

caveats: Single-arm phase 1
PD-L1 IHC assay (5H1, ≥5% threshold) differs from later companion diagnostics
Small PD-L1 biomarker subset (n=42)
Pneumonitis deaths highlighted novel, potentially fatal toxicity class
surprising_why: Durable responses in NSCLC — historically considered non-immunogenic — were contrary to prevailing assumptions and, with the melanoma data, showed PD-1 blockade has broad activity across histologies. Directly motivated the explosion of PD-1/PD-L1 trials across essentially every solid tumor.

key_finding: In metastatic urothelial carcinoma (IMvigor210) on atezolizumab, lack of response associated with a TGF-β signaling signature in peritumoral fibroblasts (F-TBRS) and a CD8+ T-cell-excluded phenotype in which T cells are trapped in collagen-rich stroma. outcome: F-TBRS predicted non-response; dual TGFβ/PD-L1 blockade converted excluded to inflamed tumors in mice
effect_size: ~298 patients with evaluable transcriptomes; non-responders elevated in pan-fibroblast TGFβ response signature; EMT6 mouse combination produced complete/near-complete regression

confidence.reasoning: Large clinical cohort, multi-modal data, independent mouse validation. TGFβ/stromal signatures replicated across subsequent datasets.

caveats: Patient correlation is associative; causal TGFβ role established in one mouse model
F-TBRS overlaps with broader stromal/EMT programs
Subsequent clinical trials of TGFβ-targeted agents (bintrafusp alfa) have largely failed to confirm therapeutic promise

human_study.effect_value: non-responders enriched for F-TBRS and T-cell-excluded phenotype

key_finding: Quadruple-mutant (Apc/Kras/Tgfbr2/Trp53) intestinal-stem-cell-driven mice develop MSS metastatic colorectal tumors with T-cell exclusion and TGFβ-activated stroma refractory to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 alone; pharmacologic TGFβ inhibition (galunisertib) unleashes Th1/CTL response that prevents metastasis; sequencing TGFβ blockade before or with anti-PD-L1 renders established liver metastases susceptible.
intervention: Galunisertib (TGFβR1 inhibitor) ± anti-PD-L1/anti-PD-1 in GEMM of metastatic MSS CRC
outcome: TGFβ blockade converted immune-excluded to T-cell-infiltrated Th1-polarized tumors; combination eradicated established liver metastases
effect_size: Dramatic regression of established liver mets with combination vs no benefit from anti-PD-1/PD-L1 alone; long-term survival

confidence.reasoning: Genetically defined GEMM recapitulating MSS CRC biology, orthogonal pharmacologic + genetic perturbations, immune depletion showing CD8 dependence; co-published with Mariathasan 2018.

caveats: Single GEMM; human MSS CRC is heterogeneous
Galunisertib oncology development discontinued
Mouse model has Tgfbr2 loss in epithelium while TGFβ is inhibited systemically; may not mirror human CRC where stromal TGFβ is dominant
surprising_why: Dramatic preclinical efficacy in MSS CRC (notoriously ICI-cold) generated major clinical enthusiasm, yet subsequent trials of TGFβ-pathway inhibitors + PD-1 in MSS CRC (bintrafusp alfa, NIS793 combinations, galunisertib + durvalumab) have produced only modest or negative results — a reproducibility gap between GEMM and human MSS CRC.

key_finding: In metastatic melanoma patients on pembrolizumab, pre-existing CD8+ T cells at the invasive tumor margin and inside the tumor, co-localized with PD-1/PD-L1 expression and a more clonal TCR repertoire, predicted response. On-treatment proliferation of intratumoral CD8+ T cells correlated with radiographic tumor shrinkage. PD-1 blockade works by reinvigorating a pre-existing adaptive immune response rather than de novo priming.
intervention: Pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) monotherapy in metastatic melanoma, pre- and on-treatment biopsies
outcome: Pre-treatment CD8 density at invasive margin predicted response; responders showed on-treatment intratumoral CD8 proliferation correlating with regression
effect_size: Baseline CD8 density at invasive margin AUC ~0.9 in discovery (n=46); validated independent cohort (n=15); TCR clonality higher in responders

confidence.reasoning: Quantitative IHC/IF on paired biopsies, independent validation, TCR sequencing support; the core finding (pre-existing CD8 predicts response) has been replicated across dozens of studies and is the basis of the 'inflamed/excluded/desert' framework.

caveats: Small single-institution cohorts (46 + 15 validation), melanoma only
IHC-based predictor not standardized; quantitative thresholds vary
Does not address responders with low baseline CD8 (~15-20%)
Pre-existing CD8 is necessary but not sufficient — many CD8-infiltrated tumors still fail

key_finding: scRNA-seq of 16,291 immune cells from 48 checkpoint-blockade-treated melanoma tumors identified two CD8+ T cell states: a memory/stem-like state marked by TCF7 associated with response/regression, and a dysfunctional/exhausted state (high inhibitory receptors, low TCF7) associated with progression. TCF7+/TCF7− CD8 ratio, and TCF7+ CD8 frequency by IF, predicted clinical outcome in an independent cohort.
intervention: Observational: anti-PD-1 and/or anti-CTLA-4 in melanoma (scRNA-seq + validation IF cohort)
outcome: TCF7+ CD8 frequency at baseline and on-treatment predicted response; epigenetic/clonal analysis supported stem-like origin
effect_size: TCF7+ CD8 frequency significantly associated with response in independent validation cohort

caveats: scRNA-seq snapshots miss rare states, subject to dropout
TCF7+ CD8 in tumors may include tumor-reactive stem-like + bystander memory; tumor-reactivity not directly verified for all TCF7+ cells
TCF7-based response prediction not standardized as a clinical assay

key_finding: The HMG-box transcription factor TOX is both necessary and sufficient to program the CD8+ T cell exhaustion transcriptional and epigenetic state during chronic antigen stimulation (LCMV Cl13 and tumor models). TOX is induced via calcineurin/NFAT2 and then acts in a feed-forward, calcineurin-independent manner; TOX-deficient CD8+ cells fail to establish the exhausted chromatin landscape, undergo terminal differentiation or death, and cannot sustain long-term responses.
intervention: Conditional Tox knockout and overexpression in mouse CD8+ T cells (LCMV chronic; tumors)
outcome: Tox loss prevented canonical exhausted CD8+ formation; Tox overexpression in effectors induced exhausted-like program
effect_size: Near-complete loss of exhausted CD8+ in Tox-KO chronic infection; large-scale ATAC-seq chromatin accessibility changes

confidence.reasoning: Multi-lab concordance (co-published with Scott 2019, Seo 2019, Yao 2019), genetic LOF/GOF, transcriptomic + epigenomic validation, consistent findings in chronic infection and tumor models.

caveats: Tox ablation impairs both exhaustion and long-term persistence — TOX-KO cells die faster
Predominantly mouse; human TOX clinical targeting remains preclinical
Exhaustion is a survival adaptation; loss of TOX may remove a restraint on effector-to-death transitions rather than unleashing durable effector function
surprising_why: Early hope was that TOX could be therapeutically antagonized to reverse exhaustion; subsequent work showed TOX-deficient exhausted cells are not better effectors but fail to persist. TOX is more accurately a cell-intrinsic survival/differentiation program under chronic antigen than a simple brake on effector function — tempering therapeutic tractability.

key_finding: A Tcf1(TCF7)+PD-1+ CD8+ T cell subset within tumors has stem-like properties, co-expressing features of central memory and exhausted cells, and is the proliferative source that expands upon checkpoint blockade; it gives rise to terminally differentiated Tcf1−PD-1+ effectors. Ablation of Tcf1+PD-1+ TILs abolishes the therapeutic response to checkpoint blockade, demonstrating ICI efficacy depends on a stem-like progenitor pool rather than on direct reinvigoration of terminally exhausted cells.
intervention: Checkpoint blockade (anti-PD-1/PD-L1, ± vaccination) in mouse tumor models; genetic ablation and Tcf7 deletion
outcome: Tcf1+PD-1+ TILs proliferate and self-renew after ICI; Tcf1 loss abrogates stem-like function; depletion of Tcf1+ TILs eliminates ICI therapeutic benefit
effect_size: Complete abrogation of checkpoint blockade efficacy upon ablation of Tcf1+ subset; the subset accounts for the proliferative burst in responders

confidence.reasoning: Convergent with Sade-Feldman 2018, Miller 2019, Im 2016 Nature; genetic perturbation + adoptive transfer establish causal role; validated in human melanoma TILs.

caveats: Mouse tumor models (B16, MC38) may not fully capture diverse human TMEs
Human Tcf1+PD-1+ cells in blood/tumor are rarer and harder to quantify
Whether Tcf1+PD-1+ cells are broadly tumor-reactive vs. include bystander memory is debated
Upstream signals maintaining the Tcf1+ progenitor pool are not resolved
surprising_why: Contradicted the then-dominant view that PD-1 blockade 'reinvigorates' exhausted effector cells; instead efficacy requires a distinct memory-like progenitor population — reframing ICI mechanism and explaining why terminally exhausted tumors fail to respond even when heavily PD-1+.

key_finding: Chen and Mellman propose the 'cancer-immune set point' framework: an individual's likelihood of responding to immunotherapy is determined by the net balance of stimulatory factors (neoantigens, T-cell infiltration, MHC expression, immunogenic cell death) and inhibitory factors (checkpoints, Tregs, MDSCs, TGFβ, metabolic barriers, microbiome) integrated across the cancer-immunity cycle. Clinically, tumors can be classified as inflamed, immune-excluded, or immune-desert, each reflecting distinct failure points that suggest tailored combinations.

confidence.reasoning: Synthesis review by originators of the cancer-immunity cycle framework; inflamed/excluded/desert taxonomy broadly adopted.

caveats: Conceptual framework; predictions must be validated empirically per tumor type
Tripartite classification simplifies heterogeneity within each category
'Set point' metaphor can mislead if interpreted as fixed; it is dynamic

key_finding: Sharma, Hu-Lieskovan, Wargo, Ribas establish the canonical taxonomy of ICI resistance: primary (tumor never responds; low TMB, antigen-presentation defects, low PD-L1, no TIL, WNT/β-catenin, PTEN loss, MYC), adaptive (tumor adapts via IFN-γ-induced PD-L1, IDO, additional checkpoints), and acquired (relapse after response; B2M loss, JAK1/2 LOF, neoantigen loss). Provides the conceptual scaffold for resistance and combination strategies.

confidence.reasoning: Authoritative synthesis by leading investigators; primary/adaptive/acquired framework is standard nomenclature in trial design and regulatory thinking.

caveats: Review without new primary data
Boundaries between primary/adaptive/acquired not always sharp in individual patients
Some specific mechanisms cited are well-documented but rare
Predates Siddiqui/Sade-Feldman stem-like CD8 biology, TOX (2019), and microbiome work (Routy/Gopalakrishnan 2018)

key_finding: In 112 melanoma patients on anti-PD-1, responders had higher gut alpha diversity and enrichment of Ruminococcaceae/Faecalibacterium; non-responders were enriched for Bacteroidales. Fecal transfer from responder patients into germ-free mice enhanced antitumor immunity and anti-PD-1 efficacy — causal support for a microbiome-immunity link.
intervention: Anti-PD-1 (nivolumab or pembrolizumab); fecal microbiota transfer into germ-free mice
outcome: Higher alpha diversity and Ruminococcaceae abundance associated with response; responder-FMT mice showed improved tumor control and increased intratumoral CD8+
effect_size: Fecal shotgun cohort n=43 (30 R vs 13 NR); alpha diversity P<0.01; Faecalibacterium abundance P<0.01

confidence.reasoning: Well-powered single-institution (MDACC) cohort with 16S + shotgun metagenomics plus mechanistic germ-free mouse transfer; Science landmark.

caveats: Single-center (MDACC, Texas) — geographic/diet bias
Small fecal shotgun sub-cohort (n=43)
Associations may reflect diet/lifestyle confounders
Specific responder taxa have not consistently replicated across geographies
surprising_why: Specific responder-associated taxa (Faecalibacterium, Ruminococcaceae) have shown inconsistent replication across independent geographic cohorts. Meta-analyses (Lee 2022, McCulloch 2022 Nat Med) found no single taxon reliably predicts anti-PD-1 response, and the Gopalakrishnan signatures often disagree with parallel Routy (Akkermansia) and Matson (Bifidobacterium) studies — underscoring cohort-specificity of the microbiome-response signal despite a robust aggregate effect.

human_study.effect_value: higher diversity & Faecalibacterium in responders

key_finding: In advanced NSCLC, RCC, and urothelial cancer on anti-PD-1/PD-L1, antibiotic exposure (within 2 months before or 1 month after ICI) shortened PFS and OS. Metagenomic stool profiling linked response to Akkermansia muciniphila; oral A. muciniphila restored anti-PD-1 efficacy after FMT from non-responders into mice via IL-12-dependent recruitment of CCR9+CXCR3+CD4+ T cells.

outcome: Antibiotics shortened OS/PFS; A. muciniphila abundance correlated with benefit; oral A. muciniphila rescued ICI efficacy in non-responder-FMT mice
effect_size: Antibiotic use associated with reduced OS (e.g., NSCLC mOS ~8 vs ~20 mo; HR ~3.5); discovery cohort ~249 patients

confidence.reasoning: Large multi-tumor cohort with metagenomic + mechanistic mouse validation; influential Science landmark.

caveats: Antibiotic analysis observational and confounded by indication
Akkermansia cutoffs/directionality not consistently replicated
Mouse MCA-205 and subcutaneous tumors may not recapitulate human epithelial cancers
FMT engraftment in mice differs from humans
surprising_why: Akkermansia muciniphila was initially presented as a clean positive biomarker, but follow-up (Derosa et al. 2022 Nat Med) showed a non-monotonic relationship — patients with very high relative abundance had worse outcomes than intermediate — complicating its use as a simple predictor. The antibiotic-harm signal has replicated more robustly than the specific Akkermansia taxonomy.

human_study.effect_value: antibiotics → shorter PFS/OS (NSCLC mOS ~8 vs ~20 mo; HR ~3.5)

Oral Bifidobacterium alone improved B16 melanoma control comparably to anti-PD-L1, and the combination nearly abolished tumor growth, acting via enhanced DC function and CD8+ priming.

outcome: Reduced B16.SIY growth; increased tumor-specific CD8+ priming and infiltration; enhanced DC activation
effect_size: Bifidobacterium-alone effect comparable to anti-PD-L1 monotherapy; combination near-complete tumor control

confidence.reasoning: Rigorous gnotobiotic/vendor-swap design, cohousing controls, FMT causality; Science landmark. Clinical translation more mixed.

caveats: Single mouse tumor model (B16) in main experiments
Bifidobacterium operationally defined by 16S at genus level
Human studies have not consistently recapitulated a Bifidobacterium-response association
Effects may reflect broader community context
surprising_why: The striking preclinical effect of a single genus has not cleanly replicated in human anti-PD-1 cohorts — Matson 2018 reported Bifidobacterium longum as response-associated in melanoma, but Gopalakrishnan (2018) and Routy (2018) highlighted different taxa. Cross-cohort meta-analyses (Lee 2022, McCulloch 2022) have not confirmed Bifidobacterium as a robust human responder marker — the mouse vendor-effect mechanism does not translate simply to heterogeneous human microbiomes.

key_finding: Antitumor efficacy of CTLA-4 blockade in mice depended on gut Bacteroides species (B. thetaiotaomicron and B. fragilis): antibiotic-treated and germ-free mice failed to respond, rescued by gavage with B. fragilis, B. fragilis polysaccharide, or adoptive transfer of B. fragilis-specific T cells. FMT from ipilimumab-treated melanoma patients into mice recapitulated the association.
intervention: Anti-CTLA-4 + microbiota manipulation (antibiotics, germ-free, B. fragilis gavage, patient-FMT)
outcome: CTLA-4 blockade lost efficacy in microbiota-depleted mice; restored by Bacteroidales exposure; T-cell responses to B. fragilis/B. theta correlated with patient efficacy
effect_size: Qualitative full loss and restoration of anti-CTLA-4 efficacy across conditions

confidence.reasoning: Multiple converging gnotobiotic and immunologic manipulations demonstrating causality in mice, plus supportive patient T cell data; co-landmark with Sivan.

caveats: CTLA-4 mouse models may not fully recapitulate human ipilimumab biology
Patient T cell response cohort small and correlative
Identified 'beneficial' Bacteroides taxa do not consistently overlap with those identified in later anti-PD-1 human cohorts
surprising_why: B. fragilis was highlighted as a beneficial CTLA-4-cooperating microbe, yet in subsequent anti-PD-1 studies (including Gopalakrishnan 2018) Bacteroidales enrichment was often associated with non-response — a sign-flip depending on checkpoint target or cohort. This discordance across CTLA-4 vs PD-1 microbiome studies has not been fully reconciled, and B. fragilis as a universal 'good' microbe has not held up.

key_finding: Phase I trial: FMT from two anti-PD-1 long-term responder donors followed by anti-PD-1 reinduction in 10 patients with anti-PD-1-refractory metastatic melanoma produced objective responses in 3 patients (1 CR, 2 PR). Responders showed donor-like gut microbiota engraftment and favorable immune changes in gut lamina propria and TME (increased CD8+ infiltration, IFN-γ signature).
intervention: FMT (colonoscopic + oral capsules) from anti-PD-1 responders + anti-PD-1 reinduction
outcome: 3/10 objective clinical responses in previously PD-1-refractory patients; donor-specific engraftment; favorable TME remodeling
effect_size: Response rate 30% (3/10) in a refractory population with expected response rate near 0%

confidence.reasoning: First-in-human randomized-donor FMT trial in Science with integrated microbiome/immune/clinical readouts. Small sample but clinical signal striking; replicated by Davar 2021.

caveats: Very small sample (n=10) with two donors
Open-label, single-arm
Anti-PD-1 reinduction alone could explain some responses, though unlikely at this rate in refractory cohort
Mechanism not resolved
surprising_why: That FMT could rescue responses in patients classified as anti-PD-1 refractory was unexpected — refractory disease had been widely assumed to reflect tumor-intrinsic immune escape (B2M/JAK loss, antigen loss), not a reversible host-microbiome state. The observation that a gut-based intervention could flip phenotype in a minority of refractory patients, alongside Davar 2021, shifted microbiome work from 'biomarker' toward 'intervention'.

key_finding: CheckMate 067 (945 untreated metastatic melanoma patients): nivolumab+ipilimumab produced substantially longer PFS than ipilimumab monotherapy, and nivolumab monotherapy was superior to ipilimumab. The combination showed its largest relative PFS benefit over nivolumab monotherapy in PD-L1-negative tumors, establishing combination PD-1 + CTLA-4 blockade as a new standard of care in advanced melanoma.

outcome: mPFS 11.5 mo (nivo+ipi) vs 6.9 mo (nivo) vs 2.9 mo (ipi); long subsequent follow-up showed durable OS benefit with combination

Generalizability to non-melanoma tumors varies

key_finding: KEYNOTE-177 phase 3 (307 treatment-naive patients, MSI-H/dMMR metastatic CRC): first-line pembrolizumab doubled median PFS versus chemotherapy (16.5 vs 8.2 months, HR 0.60) with markedly fewer grade 3+ AEs, establishing PD-1 blockade as standard first-line therapy for dMMR mCRC.

outcome: mPFS 16.5 vs 8.2 mo; ORR 43.8% vs 33.1% with far more durable responses (83% vs 35% ongoing at 24 mo)

caveats: Substantial crossover confounded OS analysis
Early progressors on pembrolizumab (~29% PD as best response) had worse outcomes than chemo in the first 6 months — sparked discussion of upfront chemo+IO
Restricted to dMMR/MSI-H subset (~4-5% of mCRC)
Heterogeneous chemotherapy comparator
surprising_why: The initial biphasic PFS curve — pembrolizumab underperforming chemotherapy in the first ~6 months before crossing over — was an unexpected pattern reflecting a substantial primary-resistance subset within dMMR mCRC, tempering the assumption that dMMR alone is a near-universal ICI predictor. The later failure to reach statistically significant OS benefit (likely due to crossover) was also a subtle disappointment.

human_study.effect_value: mPFS 16.5 vs 8.2 mo; HR 0.60

key_finding: Dual mechanism of ICI resistance in CRC: TREM2+ immunosuppressive macrophages in spatially excluded T cell-poor niches co-operate with multi-checkpoint-exhausted TIM3+LAG3+TIGIT+PD-1+ T cells to drive resistance. Colocalization of MHC+C1Q+CXCL9+ macrophages with TCF+PRF1+ T cells predicts anti-PD-1 tumor control. Quadruple blockade (PD-1 + CTLA-4 + LAG-3 + TREM2) achieves 100% clearance in dMMR and >70% in MSS orthotopic CRC models.
intervention: Anti-PD-1 ± anti-CTLA-4 ± anti-LAG-3 ± anti-TREM2 in orthotopic and patient-derived CRC models
outcome: Tumor clearance: 100% in dMMR CRC, >70% in MSS CRC with quadruple combination; spatial colocalization of myeloid-T cell niches predicts anti-PD-1 response
effect_size: >70% tumor clearance with quadruple combo vs. near-zero with anti-PD-1 monotherapy in MSS CRC models

confidence.reasoning: Robust preclinical data in orthotopic and PDX models with spatial single-cell validation; mechanism is biologically compelling and consistent with prior TREM2 and multi-exhaustion literature. Downgraded from high because no human clinical trial data yet — all efficacy evidence is preclinical.

caveats: All efficacy data preclinical (orthotopic mouse + PDX); no human clinical trial results yet
Anti-TREM2 agent used in models is not yet clinically approved
MSS CRC remains notoriously resistant; >70% clearance in models may not translate to patients
Spatial transcriptomic profiling used but spatial resolution of clinical relevance not yet established
surprising_why: TREM2-targeting was not previously combined with triple PD-1/CTLA-4/LAG-3 blockade in CRC, and the demonstration that adding myeloid re-programming breaks resistance even in MSS CRC — previously considered immune-cold and ICI-refractory — is the key novel finding.

key_finding: Pan-cancer spatial ecotype (SE) taxonomy derived from 10M+ single-cell and spatial transcriptomes identifies 9 conserved SEs with distinct geospatial TME configurations, clinical outcome associations, and differential immunotherapy response. SE profiles are recoverable non-invasively from plasma cfDNA (DNA methylation + deep learning), with cfDNA-based SE levels in ~100 melanoma patients showing striking associations with ICI response. Establishes liquid EcoTyper as a non-invasive TME spatial profiling modality.
intervention: Retrospective SE profiling via cfDNA in melanoma patients on ICI therapy
outcome: cfDNA-inferred SE levels stratify ICI responders from non-responders in melanoma cohort (~100 pts)
effect_size: Striking SE-ICI response associations in melanoma cfDNA cohort (specific HRs/ORs not yet extracted from abstract)

confidence.reasoning: Large-scale multi-cohort spatial transcriptomic atlas is methodologically rigorous (Nature, 10M+ cells). cfDNA validation in ~100 melanoma patients is clinically relevant but retrospective; prospective validation and multi-cancer cfDNA evidence not yet shown.

caveats: cfDNA SE validation cohort is melanoma-specific (~100 pts); generalizability to other tumor types not established
Retrospective design; prospective clinical utility of liquid EcoTyper not yet demonstrated
Method complexity (multi-analyte ML framework) may limit near-term clinical adoption
Specific SE thresholds and clinical decision cutoffs not yet defined
surprising_why: Non-invasive reconstruction of spatial TME ecotype state from blood cfDNA (rather than tissue biopsy) was not previously demonstrated at this scale; if prospectively validated, this would fundamentally change how ICI resistance mechanisms are characterized clinically.

human_study.n_description: ~100 melanoma patients on ICI, retrospective cfDNA cohort
human_study.effect_value: striking SE-response stratification (specific effect size pending full text)

key_finding: STING agonists unexpectedly expand immunosuppressive regulatory B cells (Bregs) in pancreatic cancer via a PI3Kγ-dependent mechanism, partially offsetting STING-driven myeloid activation. Dual targeting with SH-273/Nano-273 (STING agonist + PI3Kγ inhibitor) eliminates this Breg escape while sustaining IRF3-driven myeloid activation, extending median survival to 201 days in orthotopic pancreatic cancer models and reducing lung metastasis — outperforming either monotherapy.
intervention: SH-273 / Nano-273 (albumin nanoformulation): dual STING agonist + PI3Kγ inhibitor
outcome: Median survival 201 days; decreased lung metastasis; myeloid activation sustained; Breg expansion suppressed
effect_size: 201-day median survival (Nano-273) vs shorter with STING agonist or PI3Kγ inhibitor monotherapy (specific days not reported in abstract)

confidence.reasoning: Orthotopic mouse models only; mechanistically well-controlled with genetic perturbations confirming PI3Kγ dependence of Breg arm; no human clinical data yet

caveats: Preclinical mouse models only; no human clinical data
Specific survival comparison numbers for monotherapy arms not reported in abstract
PDAC-specific; generalizability to other ICI-resistant tumors unknown
Nano-273 formulation pharmacokinetics and toxicity in humans unknown
surprising_why: STING agonists are broadly regarded as pro-inflammatory and immunostimulatory; the finding that STING signaling paradoxically expands immunosuppressive Bregs via PI3Kγ explains partial failure of STING monotherapy and identifies a mechanistic escape route not previously recognized in the pancreatic ICI resistance literature.

key_finding: KSR2 (kinase suppressor of Ras 2) is upregulated in anti-PD-1-resistant lung cancer and acts as a central metabolic checkpoint: it enhances glucose uptake, potentiates the Warburg effect, promotes lactate accumulation, and disrupts the TCA cycle, creating an immunosuppressive TME with reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration and enriched Tregs. KSR2 knockdown resensitizes resistant tumors to anti-PD-1 therapy.
intervention: KSR2 knockdown (genetic loss-of-function) / KSR2 overexpression (gain-of-function)
outcome: KSR2 overexpression confers anti-PD-1 resistance; knockdown resensitizes; TME shows reduced CD8+ TILs and Treg enrichment

confidence.reasoning: Mouse model + correlative public clinical dataset; gain- and loss-of-function validation supports mechanistic claim; no therapeutic KSR2 inhibitor tested

caveats: Primarily mouse lung cancer models; human clinical dataset is correlative only
No KSR2-targeting therapeutic tested; clinical tractability unknown
Lung cancer focus; KSR2 role in other ICI-resistant tumor types not shown
Effect size not quantified in abstract
surprising_why: KSR2 is a scaffold protein classically studied in the Ras-RAF-MEK signaling axis for oncogenic growth; its identification as a driver of immunosuppressive metabolic reprogramming (Warburg effect → lactate → Treg enrichment) linking Ras oncogenesis directly to ICI resistance is a conceptually novel connection not previously established.

key_finding: P2RX7, an ATP-gated purinergic receptor, is required for regulatory T cells (Tregs) to accumulate in lung tumors and maintain full suppressive capacity. Tregs in both human and mouse lung tumors express elevated P2RX7; T cell-specific P2RX7 deletion reduces Treg infiltration, increases CD4+ effector T cell accumulation, improves tumor control, and reduces CTLA-4 expression on intratumoral Tregs. Pharmacological P2RX7 inhibition phenocopies genetic deletion, and higher P2RX7 expression correlates with worse survival in lung cancer patients.
intervention: T cell-specific P2RX7 knockout; pharmacological P2RX7 inhibition
outcome: Reduced Treg infiltration, decreased CTLA-4 on Tregs, increased CD4+ effector T cells, improved tumor control in mouse lung cancer models
effect_size: Reduced tumor growth and Treg infiltration in P2RX7-KO and inhibitor-treated mice; quantitative effect sizes not available from accessible abstract

confidence.reasoning: Single study; rigorous in vivo genetic and pharmacological evidence in mouse lung cancer; human correlative data (expression + survival) supporting clinical relevance; not yet validated in ICI-treated patient cohorts.

caveats: Lung cancer models only; pan-tumor generalization of P2RX7-Treg axis unconfirmed.
P2RX7 inhibitors (e.g., AZ10606120) are not clinically approved; montelukast does not target P2RX7.
Human data are correlative (expression/survival); direct ICI combination efficacy in patients untested.
surprising_why: P2RX7 in Tregs connects tumor metabolic stress (extracellular ATP from dying cells) to Treg persistence and CTLA-4 upregulation — an unexpected molecular bridge between immunogenic cell death signaling and immune suppression. Mechanistically distinct from and potentially complementary to anti-CTLA-4 antibody, which depletes Tregs via FcR-mediated ADCC.

key_finding: Cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 (CysLTR1) drives a tumor-promoting myelopoiesis program that recruits immunosuppressive neutrophils and myeloid cells to the tumor microenvironment, conferring resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Genetic deletion or pharmacological blockade of CysLTR1 with the FDA-approved asthma drug montelukast reprograms these cells from immunosuppressive to immunostimulatory phenotypes, slowing tumor growth, improving survival, and restoring anti-PD-1 efficacy — including in models with acquired ICI resistance — across five cancer types (TNBC, melanoma, ovarian cancer, colon cancer, prostate cancer). Findings were validated in human immune cells, human tumor tissue, and patient cancer datasets.
intervention: CysLTR1 genetic deletion; montelukast (FDA-approved CysLTR1 antagonist) combined with anti-PD-1
outcome: Myeloid cell reprogramming to immunostimulatory phenotype; slower tumor growth; improved survival; restored ICI response including in acquired-resistance tumors
effect_size: Tumor growth reduction and survival improvement demonstrated across five mouse cancer models; quantitative effect sizes not confirmed from press reports

confidence.reasoning: Single study published today; rigorous genetic + pharmacological evidence across five syngeneic mouse tumor types; human tissue and dataset validation supporting translational relevance; not yet tested in patients.

caveats: Survival/tumor-growth data from mouse syngeneic models; human efficacy data are tissue/dataset-correlative only.
Optimal montelukast dosing for cancer vs. asthma doses unknown.
Study is newly published (May 19, 2026); independent replication pending.
Mechanism of myeloid reprogramming (specific downstream signaling of CysLTR1 in myeloid progenitors) not fully characterized in available reports.
surprising_why: CysLTR1 (targeted by FDA-approved montelukast) acts systemically at the level of bone marrow myelopoiesis, not just locally in the tumor — suggesting resistance can be reversed by reprogramming myeloid cell fate before tumor entry. The "reprogramming" rather than "depletion" of tumor-promoting neutrophils is conceptually novel: existing strategies (CXCR2 blockade, CSF1R blockade) deplete myeloid cells, but CysLTR1 blockade re-educates them into tumor-fighting cells.

key_finding: Meta-analysis of seven ICI-treated advanced melanoma cohorts (n=678) identifies Faecalibacterium and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) biosynthesis pathways as the most reproducible microbiome features associated with response. Cross-cohort functional pathway analysis (SCFA production) shows higher reproducibility than taxon-level analysis alone. Akkermansia shows non-monotonic patterns. Faecalibacterium-SCFA association was consistent across different ICI regimens within the melanoma setting.
intervention: anti-PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint blockade (multiple regimens)
outcome: Improved ICI response rate in melanoma patients with higher Faecalibacterium and SCFA-producing bacteria
effect_size: Faecalibacterium enrichment and SCFA functional pathway most reproducible cross-cohort signal (specific effect sizes meta-analytic summary)

confidence.reasoning: Meta-analysis of 7 observational cohort studies; heterogeneous ICI regimens, microbiome methods, and patient populations; melanoma-specific; lacks prospective interventional validation of SCFA pathway

caveats: Melanoma-specific — pan-cancer generalizability not demonstrated
Observational cohorts; causal role of SCFA pathway requires interventional validation
Different microbiome profiling methods across cohorts (16S vs shotgun metagenomics)
Does not establish Faecalibacterium reproducibility outside melanoma context

human_study.feature: Faecalibacterium abundance and SCFA production pathway enrichment in gut microbiome
human_study.effect_value: Faecalibacterium / SCFA pathway most reproducible cross-cohort signal
human_study.method: Meta-analysis (16S rRNA + shotgun metagenomics + functional pathway analysis)

key_finding: In a phase 2 basket trial of pembrolizumab across 154 patients with advanced rare cancers (ORR 14.8%; CBR 26.8%), pre-existing CD3+/CD8+ T cell infiltrate and active T cell signaling predicted clinical benefit. A subset of tumors with moderate baseline immune infiltration that showed inducible immune recruitment during treatment also derived benefit. TME features provided predictive value beyond TMB and MSI-H status.
intervention: pembrolizumab monotherapy
outcome: Clinical benefit (ORR + stable disease ≥24 wk); overall response rate 14.8%
effect_size: ORR 14.8%; CBR 26.8%; pre-existing CD8+ infiltrate and inducible recruitment associated with response

Biomarker analysis exploratory/unvalidated

key_finding: Cancer-induced nerve injury (CINI) drives anti-PD-1 resistance across cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma and gastric cancer: invading cancer cells degrade peripheral nerve myelin sheaths, triggering IL-6- and type I IFN-mediated neuronal repair inflammation that chronically suppresses the TME and impairs CD8+ T cell function. This resistance programme is reversible by combining anti-PD-1 with anti-IL-6R blockade, by denervation, or by genetic ablation of Atf3 or Ifnar1 in neurons.
intervention: Anti-PD-1 ± anti-IL-6R blockade; also tested: tumour denervation, Atf3-cKO, Ifnar1-KO
outcome: PNI/CINI correlates with poor anti-PD-1 response in three tumour types; anti-IL-6R + anti-PD-1 combination rescues anti-tumour immunity in mouse models
effect_size: Qualitative: PNI/CINI+ patients enriched among ICI non-responders across three tumour types

confidence.reasoning: Multi-tumour-type clinical validation in Nature; genetically tractable mouse models (Atf3/Ifnar1 conditional KO); mechanism independently validated at multiple intervention points; replicated across cSCC, melanoma, gastric cancer

caveats: Specific clinical effect sizes (HR, ORR) not available from abstract
Anti-IL-6R/anti-PD-1 combination benefit not yet shown in prospective trials
PNI is assessed histologically and not routinely quantified across all tumour types
surprising_why: Peripheral nerve injury as a driver of systemic TME immunosuppression was not previously recognised in ICI resistance; injured neurons autonomously initiate IL-6/IFN-β inflammation that chronically suppresses antitumour immunity, reframing perineural invasion from an anatomical predictor to an active immune-evasion mechanism with a druggable counterpart.

human_study.effect_value: PNI/CINI+ patients enriched among anti-PD-1 non-responders

key_finding: TMEM87A is a Golgi-localized transmembrane protein that maintains Golgi pH homeostasis and suppresses ferroptosis by preserving FSP1-mediated reduction of coenzyme Q; TMEM87A ablation induces Golgi overacidification, sensitises tumour cells to lipid-peroxidation-driven ferroptosis, enhances antitumour T cell responses, and potentiates PD-1 blockade in melanoma, CRC and HCC in vivo. Tumoral TMEM87A expression negatively correlates with ICI response and survival in patient cohorts.
intervention: TMEM87A genetic ablation (KO/knockdown) ± anti-PD-1
outcome: Tumour growth suppression, enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration, potentiated PD-1 blockade efficacy in melanoma, CRC, HCC mouse models; TMEM87A-high expression → worse ICI outcomes in patients
effect_size: Qualitative: TMEM87A high expression negatively correlates with ICI response; specific effect sizes not available

confidence.reasoning: Mechanistically rigorous across three tumour types in mouse models; clinical correlation present (retrospective IHC); Nature Cancer publication; PMID not yet confirmed (DOI used as canonical ID)

caveats: Mouse preclinical models for efficacy; clinical data is retrospective IHC correlation
No human interventional data; TMEM87A inhibitors not clinically available
Whether ferroptosis induction in the context of TMEM87A loss affects non-tumour cells is not addressed
surprising_why: Golgi apparatus pH homeostasis as a ferroptosis checkpoint linking tumour-intrinsic biology to ICI efficacy is unexpected; extends the ferroptosis-ICI connection beyond GPX4/FSP1 lipid peroxide metabolism to organelle-level pH regulation via a transmembrane protein not previously implicated in immune evasion.

human_study.effect_value: TMEM87A high → worse ICI response and survival outcome

Metastatic but not primary tumour samples are predictive.

outcome: Spatial TME features predict ICI response; border T cell infiltration and immune diversity are top predictors; primary tumour samples are uninformative
effect_size: SpaceCat spatial features outperform PD-L1 IHC (specific AUC/HR not available from abstract)

confidence.reasoning: 103 patients from a prospective phase 2 trial (TONIC); multiplexed imaging is rigorous; but single trial, single cancer type (TNBC), and specific effect sizes not quantified in available summary; needs external validation

caveats: Single phase 2 trial (TONIC); independent TNBC cohort validation required
SpaceCat pipeline not yet clinically deployable
N=103 limits feature-level statistical power
Nivolumab single-agent in TNBC is not standard of care (typically combined with chemo)

key_finding: GIV/Girdin (CCDC88A) is a macrophage-intrinsic endocytic adaptor that binds PD-1 via a conserved TILL loop interaction, enabling clathrin-mediated internalization of PD-1 from tumour-associated macrophage (TAM) surfaces. GIV loss traps PD-1 at the plasma membrane, collapses macrophage effector function, drives hyperprogressive disease under checkpoint blockade, and abolishes therapeutic benefit. Psychotropic drugs that inhibit endocytosis phenocopy GIV loss and accelerate tumour growth in mouse models, identifying a clinically relevant drug-interaction vulnerability.
intervention: Anti-PD-1 checkpoint blockade; GIV/CCDC88A genetic deletion; pharmacological endocytosis inhibitors; psychotropic drugs
outcome: GIV deletion → PD-1 surface accumulation on TAMs → hyperprogressive disease under anti-PD-1; psychotropic drugs → similar phenotype
effect_size: Qualitative: GIV KO converts therapeutic benefit to hyperprogression in mouse tumour models

confidence.reasoning: Mechanistically compelling with defined molecular interaction (TILL-loop GIV-PD1); preprint, not yet peer reviewed; mouse models only; no human validation of GIV expression on TAMs or its prognostic relevance; capped at medium per preprint guideline

caveats: Preprint, not yet peer reviewed
Human validation of GIV expression on TAMs and clinical correlates not reported
Psychotropic drug effects require clinical epidemiological validation
PD-1 on macrophages has distinct biology from T cell PD-1; generalizability to T cell biology unclear
surprising_why: PD-1 is canonically studied on T cells; the finding that macrophage-intrinsic PD-1 endocytosis determines immunotherapy outcome reframes the mechanism of checkpoint blockade; moreover, that disrupting this endocytic checkpoint converts therapy into hyperprogression — and that psychotropic drugs commonly used in cancer patients can trigger this — is clinically alarming and entirely novel.

key_finding: CD40 agonist antibody repolarises monocytes and macrophages towards a proinflammatory phenotype and reduces tumour growth / improves survival in B2m-null melanoma and colorectal cancer mouse models that are resistant to anti-PD-1 therapy via antigen-presentation deficiency. The rescue is CD8+ T cell-independent. Single-cell RNA-seq reveals accumulation of immunosuppressive macrophages in B2m-null tumours; human RNA-seq analysis confirms enrichment of inflammatory monocyte signatures in ICI responders.
intervention: Anti-CD40 agonist antibody (± anti-PD-1 in combination experiments)
outcome: Tumour growth reduction and improved survival in B2m-null models; myeloid reprogramming from immunosuppressive to proinflammatory phenotype without requiring T cell antigen recognition
effect_size: Qualitative: CD40 agonist restores tumour control in B2m-null models resistant to anti-PD-1

confidence.reasoning: Mouse models with scRNA-seq mechanistic depth; human RNA-seq dataset correlation adds translational signal; preprint, not peer reviewed; CD40 agonists are in clinical development; capped at medium for preprint

caveats: Preprint, not yet peer reviewed
Mouse models only for efficacy; human evidence is correlational dataset analysis only
CD40 agonists have challenging toxicity profiles (cytokine release) in clinical trials
Whether this specifically rescues the B2m-null patient subset requires human prospective validation
surprising_why: Prior paradigm held that B2m LOF acquired resistance — which prevents antigen presentation to CD8+ T cells — was therapeutically untreatable by immune-based approaches; demonstrating that myeloid reprogramming via CD40 activation controls these tumours entirely without T cell antigen recognition establishes a CD8-independent rescue mechanism for the most definitively resistance-driving molecular lesion in the field.

key_finding: In 181 ICB-treated GBM patients profiled by bulk DNA/RNA sequencing and single-nucleus RNA-seq, the mesenchymal (MES) transcriptional subtype at baseline predicts improved overall survival on ICB (but not standard chemoradiation), associated with high HLA-I expression and greater T cell infiltration. Transition from MES to a non-mesenchymal transcriptional state is the molecular correlate of acquired ICB resistance.
intervention: Immune checkpoint blockade (PD-1/PD-L1)
outcome: Improved OS in MES GBM following ICB but not chemoradiation; non-MES transition marks acquired ICB resistance
effect_size: MES subtype associates with improved OS on ICB versus non-MES (magnitude not stated in available data)

confidence.reasoning: Observational cohort (n=181); multi-omic profiling adds mechanistic depth; no randomization; abstract-level data only; GBM overall ICB response rate is low

caveats: Retrospective observational study; cannot establish causality
Overall ICI response rate in GBM remains low even in MES subtype
Transcriptional subtyping not routinely clinically available
Non-MES transition may reflect immune-selection of pre-existing non-MES clones rather than active transcriptional reprogramming
surprising_why: Mesenchymal GBM, classically considered more aggressive and immunosuppressive, shows paradoxically better ICB response than non-mesenchymal subtypes — explained by higher HLA-I expression and T cell infiltration; suggests that certain immunosuppressive transcriptional programs co-occur with immune accessibility in this tumour type.

key_finding: Tumor cell-intrinsic Argonaute 2 (Ago2) suppresses STAT1-mediated IFN-γ signaling in NSCLC, creating an immunorefractory phenotype resistant to ICI; genetic deletion of Ago2 restores interferon signaling, upregulates CCL2 and CXCL10, promotes myeloid and T cell TME recruitment, and converts Lewis lung carcinoma tumors from ICI-resistant to ICI-sensitive (3.5-fold growth reduction at day 18); high Ago2 combined with a low IFN gene signature correlates with worse survival in NSCLC patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors.
intervention: Genetic Ago2 deletion in tumor cells
outcome: 3.5-fold decrease in tumor growth at day 18 in delta-Ago2 tumors with ICI versus wild-type; restored T cell and myeloid infiltration via CCL2/CXCL10 upregulation; patient survival correlation with Ago2/IFN signature
effect_size: 3.5-fold growth reduction (delta-Ago2 + ICI vs. WT + ICI, day 18)

confidence.reasoning: Peer-reviewed PLOS Biology; murine LLC syngeneic model data with patient cohort correlation; single study from one group; no human interventional data; Ago2 is a pleiotropic RISC component with broad post-transcriptional roles

caveats: Primary mechanistic experiments in LLC (Lewis lung carcinoma) syngeneic mouse model; generalizability to human NSCLC subtypes or other tumor types unconfirmed
Patient data is retrospective biomarker correlation; N and specific effect sizes not available from abstract
Ago2 is a core RISC component with broad post-transcriptional functions; therapeutic targeting may have off-target consequences beyond IFN-γ/STAT1
surprising_why: Ago2 has been primarily characterized as an oncogene driving tumor-intrinsic growth signals; this study repositions it as a post-transcriptional suppressor of STAT1-mediated IFN-γ signaling and ICI sensitivity, a mechanism mechanistically distinct from canonical JAK/STAT genetic LOF resistance and unexpectedly implicating microRNA machinery in the IFN-resistance axis.

key_finding: BET bromodomain inhibitors (BETis) reinvigorate exhausted CD8+ T cells from primary malignant pleural effusions of lung cancer patients by activating the MYC-ODC1 polyamine biosynthesis axis, expanding intracellular polyamine pools and altering chromatin accessibility. Single-cell RNA-seq demonstrates a shift from terminal toward progenitor-like exhausted T cells; ODC1 genetic or pharmacological inhibition abolishes the reinvigoration effect, establishing polyamine metabolism as the proximate signal.
intervention: BET bromodomain inhibitors (BETis)
outcome: Reinvigoration of exhausted T cells; shift from terminal to progenitor-exhausted phenotype; enhanced effector function in lung cancer patient-derived primary cells
effect_size: ODC1 inhibition (genetic and pharmacological) completely ablates BETi-mediated T cell reinvigoration; scRNA-seq shows quantitative shift in exhaustion trajectory

confidence.reasoning: Multi-omic validation (scRNA-seq, transcriptomics, metabolomics, ATAC-seq) in primary patient-derived T cells; ODC1 rescue confirms mechanism; published in Nature Immunology; caveat: ex vivo only, no in vivo animal or clinical validation

caveats: All experiments performed ex vivo on malignant pleural effusion-derived T cells; no in vivo (mouse or patient) validation reported
No clinical outcome data; mechanism-to-clinical-benefit link requires testing
Lung cancer-specific; generalizability to other tumor types with different metabolic microenvironments is untested
surprising_why: The mechanism is not direct epigenetic reversal of exhaustion transcription factors (TOX, NFAT) but rather metabolic: BETi activates MYC → ODC1 → polyamine biosynthesis, and polyamine pool expansion is the proximate T cell reinvigoration signal; ODC1 is primarily known as a cancer cell metabolism enzyme, not as a T cell immunotherapy target.

key_finding: Immune cell-intrinsic STING activation drives paracrine tumor ferroptosis in CRC: TBK1 phosphorylates cPLA2 at Ser505, releasing arachidonic acid (AA) into the TME; adjacent CRC cells take up AA, which inhibits EP300-mediated ACSL4 K426 lactylation and promotes ACSL4-dependent ferroptosis; STING agonist synergizes with anti-PD-1 via this immune-to-tumor ferroptosis relay.
intervention: STING agonist + anti-PD-1
outcome: Tumor ferroptosis and enhanced anti-tumor immunity in CRC preclinical models

confidence.reasoning: PNAS peer-reviewed; mechanistically detailed biochemical cascade (TBK1→cPLA2→AA→ACSL4 lactylation) implying multiple validation steps; but limited to CRC preclinical models without patient cohort data. ACSL4 lactylation at K426 is a novel post-translational modification node requiring independent replication.

caveats: No patient cohort data; purely preclinical
Single tumor type (CRC)
ACSL4 K426 lactylation as the regulatory node needs independent replication
surprising_why: The ferroptosis-sensitizing signal originates in the immune compartment (STING in immune cells) and is transmitted paraculturally to tumor cells via a lipid mediator (arachidonic acid), making this mechanistically distinct from the autocrine IFN-γ→IRF1→AGPAT3 ferroptosis axis already in the synthesis; and ACSL4 lactylation as the switch is a novel PTM node not previously linked to ferroptosis regulation.

Direct human clinical validation absent
Specific microbial taxa or pathways driving the enhanced anti-PD-1 effect not fully characterized
surprising_why: The obesity paradox (high BMI → better ICI response) is mediated by diet-specific gut microbiome features rather than by metabolic or adipose-derived signals; the benefit can be reproduced by dietary modification or FMT without obesity — decoupling the ICI sensitization signal from bodyweight itself.

key_finding: PID1 (phosphotyrosine interaction domain-containing protein 1) maintains immunosuppressive tumor-associated macrophage identity by limiting LDL receptor expression and oxysterol production; PID1 deficiency in myeloid cells upregulates LDL receptor, driving oxysterol generation that switches macrophage fate from immunosuppressive to antitumoral phenotypes, improving anti-PD-1 efficacy; pan-cancer human TAM data show elevated PID1 correlated with immunosuppressive gene signatures.
intervention: PID1 genetic deletion in myeloid cells; oxysterol pathway targeting
outcome: Macrophage fate switch from immunosuppressive to antitumoral; improved anti-PD-1 efficacy in mouse tumor models
